name: Ogee curve analysis
lead: In aesthetic facial surgery, the ogee curve describes the S-shaped line running from the cheekbone (malar prominence) down into the mid-cheek hollow [1]. The word comes from geometry, where an ogee is an S-shaped curve joining a concave arc to a convex arc, and it is also used in architecture and engineering [1].

Mid-face rejuvenation in the surgical literature often aims to restore or smooth this curve [1]. Filler papers describe a smooth ogee curve, along with an oval face, pronounced cheekbones and a defined jawline, as global aesthetic goals [2][3]. On looksmax.org the curve is analyzed as a feature separating more attractive faces from average ones [4].

The curve depends on both bone and soft tissue: the cheekbone (zygomatic bone) forms the prominence, while volume or loss of volume in the mid-cheek determines how deep the hollow beneath it appears. People who want a more pronounced curve therefore look at bone-based options such as cheek implants, volume-based options such as hyaluronic acid filler or fat grafting, and leaner-face approaches such as lowering body fat or removing buccal fat [6][8][9].

Where the cheek contour comes from also explains why it changes with age and weight: the youthful midface is described as having volume over the cheekbone that tapers smoothly into the cheek, whereas loss of volume or descent of the cheek fat reads as a flatter or hollower profile, which is why mid-face rejuvenation is framed as restoring the curve rather than creating something new.[1][9]

paras: Geometrically, an ogee has a concave arc and a convex arc meeting at an inflection point, with end tangents roughly parallel; it appears in Gothic arches, mouldings, ship hulls, dam spillways and aircraft wing design [1]. In facial aesthetics the term borrows that shape for the cheek profile [1].

Ogee forms appear in textiles from the 12th century and are associated with Gothic and Gothic Revival architecture, where mirrored ogees meet at an apex to form the ogee arch; a reversed form, the cyma reversa, appears in antiquity and the profile is common in decorative mouldings.[1]

The zygomatic (malar) bone forms the cheekbone, contributes to the lateral wall and floor of the orbit and to the zygomatic arch, and gives attachment to the zygomaticus muscle and the masseter [8]. Wikipedia notes that prominent zygomatic arches are considered physically attractive in some cultures, in both men and women, and that some people undergo cheek augmentation for this reason [8]. The masseter, which the forum thread links to the curve, attaches to the lower border of the zygomatic bone [8][4].

In facial plastic surgery, the aim of a mid-face rejuvenation is described as restoring the ogee curve and enhancing the cheekbones, which are common parts of routine facelift surgery [1]. A midface lift uses small incisions along the hairline and inside the mouth to lift and reposition the fat layer over the cheekbones, which can improve cheekbone contour and the lines between nose and mouth [9]. Facelift techniques have developed since the first reported procedure in Berlin in 1901, with the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) described in 1976 and subperiosteal approaches in 1979 [9].

Non-surgical approaches described in the filler literature use hyaluronic acid at the cheek and infraorbital region to restore the curve; one technique paper describes injecting 0.5 to 1 mL of hyaluronic acid filler at marked anatomical points to make infraorbital filling more reproducible [7], and another describes newer injection points intended to reach a smooth ogee curve without a bulky look [5]. An Indian-face paper notes that the width of the malar prominences and mandibular angles is smaller than in other Asian and Caucasian populations and that soft tissue is heavier, which shapes planning [2].

Cheek augmentation by implant uses solid silicone, porous polyethylene or expanded PTFE placed over the cheekbone. Malar implants add projection directly on the bone, submalar implants address a sunken midface, and combined implants cover both; implants are usually placed through an incision inside the upper mouth and are often paired with a facelift or chin augmentation.[11] Cited risks include infection, bleeding, asymmetry, implant displacement, temporary loss of sensation, and difficult removal when tissue grows into porous material.[11] Cutting and repositioning the cheekbone itself is described as rare and used mostly in reconstructive surgery.[11]

Hyaluronic acid fillers and a patient's own fat are the less invasive routes to cheek volume; both are described as eventually resorbing, with fat regarded as more lasting.[11] Technique papers in the filler literature treat the curve as a planning target, for instance by selecting injection points meant to reach a smooth ogee without a bulky result.[5]

Because the hollow under the cheekbone reads more clearly when the lower cheek is leaner, people also discuss weight loss and buccal fat removal. The buccal fat pad is a deep fat pad lying between the buccinator and superficial muscles such as the masseter and zygomaticus, and it is linked in anatomical descriptions to hollow cheeks and the nasolabial fold; Wikipedia states that it loses volume between childhood and adulthood and that removal carries a risk of damage to the buccal branch of the facial nerve and the parotid duct.[10] Both a looksmax.org thread and the anatomy source place the pad in the same region as the curve, while an account in that thread of a self-performed removal that went wrong illustrates the reported hazards.[4][10]

No studies found testing the ogee curve as a predictor of attractiveness. Published case reports and technique papers use it as a treatment goal: a filler paper describes injection points intended to achieve a smooth ogee curve while avoiding bulkiness [5], another discusses fillers for an Indian face with different skeletal and soft tissue proportions [2], and a retrospective comparative study of amniotic allograft implantation versus platelet-rich plasma addressed midface aging correction [6]. A paper on infraorbital hyaluronic acid injection technique also addresses the region [7].

A widely viewed looksmax.org thread by the user Clavicular says the ogee curve is extremely important for attractiveness in men and women, and attributes the shape to the zygomatic bones, gonions and masseter muscles [4]. The thread also covers buccal fat removal and other methods, and mentions an account of a self-performed buccal fat removal that went wrong [4]. Responses in the thread were largely positive [4].

In this vocabulary the curve is treated as one more measurable feature of the midface, discussed alongside cheekbone height, gonial angle and buccal fat as parts of a lean, sculpted lower face.[4] The geometric origin of the word is part of the appeal: members use it to name a contour that photographs and mirrors make easy to compare, and the surgical literature uses the same word for the same S-shaped transition.[1][4]

lore.intro: The ogee curve is promoted on looksmax.org as a key feature, with the thread's author ranking it among the most important for attractiveness [4].

claims.claim: A clear ogee curve separates a "chad" from a "normie".
claims.believers: The thread's author says the curve is extremely important for attractiveness in men and women, and explains it through zygomatic projection, gonial shape and the masseter [4].
claims.experts: Surgical papers describe a smooth ogee curve as an aesthetic goal in filler and midface work [2][5], but no study found tests it as a determinant of attractiveness.

card.summary: The S-shaped line from cheekbone to cheek hollow, used as a goal in filler surgery and as a hotly promoted beauty marker online.
card.note: Appears as a treatment goal in filler papers; no study tests it as a driver of attractiveness.

quick.overview:
The ogee curve is the S-shaped contour from the cheekbone into the hollow of the mid-cheek. Surgeons talk about restoring it in midface rejuvenation.

Looksmax.org members call it a major feature for attractiveness. No study tested that claim.
quick.mechanism: Forum members tie the curve to zygomatic projection, gonial flare and masseter size. Clinicians describe adjusting it with fillers or other midface volume treatments.
quick.risks: The concept itself is descriptive. Procedures used to pursue it, such as fillers or buccal fat removal, carry their own risks; forums also contain accounts of a self-performed buccal fat removal that went wrong.

chain: Prominent cheekbone sits above a gently hollowed mid-cheek
The face reads as an S-shaped line in three-quarter view
angle.text: The curve is used as a way to read and plan the mid-face: a visible S-line from cheekbone to cheek hollow is treated as a sign of a defined, youthful face. People pursue it through filler, midface surgery, or leaner-face methods.
